old: Addition–elimination is fastest at a carbon ortho or para to NO2, because the Meisenheimer anion can put its charge on the nitro oxygens. F is ortho to NO2; Br is meta to it, so the bromine is not activated. Fluoride is also the best SNAr leaving group because its electronegativity speeds the rate-determining addition step. The product is N,N-dimethyl-4-bromo-2-nitroaniline.
new: Addition–elimination is fastest at a carbon ortho or para to NO2, because the Meisenheimer anion can put its charge on the nitro oxygens. F is ortho to NO2; Br is meta to it, so the bromine is not activated. Fluoride is also the best SNAr leaving group because its electronegativity speeds the rate-determining addition step. The product is 4-bromo-N,N-dimethyl-2-nitroaniline.
why: IUPAC alphabetical order: bromo before dimethyl (N,N-dimethyl alphabetized under m)

old: 6 would fit an ortho or meta isomer with partial symmetry; the para isomer has two equivalent pairs, giving 5.
new: 6 treats only one pair of ring CH carbons as equivalent. In the para isomer the mirror plane makes both pairs (C2/C6 and C3/C5) equivalent, giving 5; the ortho and meta isomers have no symmetry and give 7.
why: Old text claimed ortho/meta isomers with partial symmetry give 6; both have 7 distinct carbons

old: The Diels–Alder reaction gives methyl cyclohex-3-ene-1-carboxylate: the ester carbon is C1 and the new C=C is C3=C4. Ozonolysis with a reductive workup cuts C3=C4 into two CHO groups and opens the ring. C1 is then joined to C2–C3 (CH2CHO) on one side and C6–C5–C4 (CH2CH2CHO) on the other: methyl 2-(2-oxoethyl)-5-oxopentanoate.
new: The Diels–Alder reaction gives methyl cyclohex-3-ene-1-carboxylate: the ester carbon is C1 and the new C=C is C3=C4. Ozonolysis with a reductive workup cuts C3=C4 into two CHO groups and opens the ring. C1 is then joined to C2–C3 (CH2CHO) on one side and C6–C5–C4 (CH2CH2CHO) on the other: methyl 5-oxo-2-(2-oxoethyl)pentanoate.
why: Substituent prefixes alphabetized: oxo before oxoethyl

old: This swaps II and III. The bromide route loses the heavier by-product share (49% vs 55%), so it is the lowest.
new: This swaps II and III. The bromide route has the lower atom economy (49% vs 55%) because the heavy Br atom leaves in NaBr, so it is the lowest.
why: 49%/55% are atom economies, not by-product shares

old: Cyclization uses the C5 OH, so C2–C5 keep their configurations: in D-allose all four are R in the open chain, and in the pyranose C2, C3 and C5 are R while C4 is S. The β anomer has the C1 OH cis to the C5 CH2OH (C1 is R). The correct structure has C1 R, C2 R, C3 R, C4 S, C5 R: β-D-allopyranose. In a Haworth drawing, all four ring OH groups and the CH2OH point up.
new: Cyclization uses the C5 OH, so C2–C5 keep their configurations: in D-allose all four are R in the open chain, and in the pyranose C2, C3 and C5 are R while C4 is labeled S (ring closure changes its priorities, not its geometry). The β anomer has the C1 OH cis to the C5 CH2OH (C1 is R). The correct structure has C1 R, C2 R, C3 R, C4 S, C5 R: β-D-allopyranose. In a Haworth drawing, the C1 OH and the CH2OH point up, while the C2, C3 and C4 OH groups (all on the right in the Fischer projection) point down.
why: Fischer right-side OH = Haworth down; beta-D-allopyranose has C2–C4 OH down. Also clarify C4 R->S is a CIP priority change
